findings.message: From a competitor product perspective, the plan completely fails to define how it will identify what constitutes an 'AI swarm' versus a normal user process. Wave 1 specifies WMI discovery but lacks any fingerprinting rules, telemetry hooks, or heuristic engines to differentiate a standard VS Code instance or terminal from an AI-driven one (Anchor, cowork). Without AI-specific detection logic, this tool has no moat and is functionally identical to a generic OS task manager.

Wave 5 proposes a 'violation explanation template generator' for the 'Show Context' toggle, but the architecture outlines no mechanism to extract actual AI context (e.g., active prompts, workspace context, or agent IDs) from the target processes. A competitor product would show exactly what the AI is trying to do; providing only a generic boilerplate template without a data-extraction pipeline fails the requirement for a 'detailed, human-readable explanation of what the process is'.

Wave 1 proposes WMI for real-time system-wide process discovery, while Wave 6 uses ETW for historical telemetry. Competitor endpoint and monitoring tools avoid WMI for continuous enumeration due to its severe CPU overhead, slow response times, and general fragility. Failing to use lightweight ETW or modern native APIs for real-time tracking will degrade user system performance and make the sentinel too heavy to run continuously.

While Objective 4 specifies freezing the swarm pending human approval, suspending processes retains their memory and VRAM allocations. If a zombie swarm is consuming massive resources, freezing it without a fast-path to reclaim resources leaves the user's system crippled until manual intervention. Competitors would implement a memory-reclamation strategy or prominently warn the user about resource locking during the freeze state.

findings.section: Wave 1 — System-Wide Process Discovery and Daemon Core
findings.message: You are selling a system-wide AI sentinel, but Wave 1 only implements generic WMI process discovery. Any intern can list Windows processes. How do you actually fingerprint an 'AI-related process' (e.g., distinguishing a VS Code AI swarm from a standard VS Code instance)? Without defining the specific heuristics or command-line signatures for Anchor, VS Code, and cowork, you are just building an expensive Task Manager. The core detection IP is completely missing from the plan.

findings.section: Wave 6 — Historical Forensics UI and Resource Bounding
findings.message: You've spent all your planning effort on background thread CPU limits and ETW chunking, but entirely skipped the actual intelligence: how does the system know a past process actually 'evaded detection' and was a 'zombie swarm' rather than just a legitimate high-CPU compile job? Without a concrete heuristic to correlate resource consumption with evasion, this feature will just be a noisy, useless history log that delivers zero actionable value.

findings.section: Wave 1 — System-Wide Process Discovery and Daemon Core
findings.message: The plan specifies WMI for process discovery but fails to define a signature registry or heuristic classification engine. A future maintainer needs a clear, updateable mechanism (e.g., regex patterns, command-line arguments, parent-child process chains) to distinguish an 'AI-related process' from a normal user process. Without this, the system will drown in false positives, making it unmaintainable.

findings.section: Wave 5 — Bulk Swarm Approvals, Context Display, and Lifecycle Management
findings.message: The plan implements 'freezing' a rogue swarm but ignores the severe OS-level risks of suspending a process tree. If a suspended AI swarm process holds shared IPC locks, file handles, or UI threads (especially relevant for VS Code integrations), it will cause cascading deadlocks on the host OS. A maintainer will be unable to safely debug or resolve these freezes without a defined safe-suspend orchestration strategy or timeout fallback.

findings.section: Wave 6 — Historical Forensics UI and Resource Bounding
findings.message: The offline analysis bounds CPU (5%) and RAM (250MB), but completely ignores disk storage and I/O for system-wide ETW telemetry. ETW logs grow exponentially. Without a strict retention policy, log rotation, or circular buffer configuration defined in the plan, the feature will silently bloat the user's hard drive, leading to critical maintenance overhead and user complaints.
